# Loaded LNG Tankers from Qatar Turn Back Before Hormuz Crossing

Maritime Activity Reports, Inc.

April 6, 2026

© Kalyakan / Adobe Stock

Two vessels loaded with liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Ras Laffan, Qatar, turned back after they moved eastward towards the Strait of Hormuz, ship-tracking data showed on Monday.

Had the vessels successfully crossed the strait, it would have been the first transit of LNG cargoes through the waterway since the U.S.-Israel war with Iran began on February 28. [...] Offshore • Middle East • Asia • LNG Tankers • Oil and Gas • War • Strait of Hormuz

# Hormuz standoff forces Qatar LNG tankers to turn back

April 06, 2026

(Bloomberg) — Two liquefied natural gas tankers from Qatar in the Persian Gulf have switched to Pakistan as their next destinations after appearing to abort an earlier attempt to leave via the Strait of Hormuz. [...] Transit through Hormuz would be a shot in the arm for Qatar, which supplied nearly a fifth of all LNG last year, even as the country’s Ras Laffan export plant has been shut for over a month due to Iranian attacks. This could allow Qatar to send more shipments that are already loaded and waiting within the Persian Gulf, or offload fuel from storage.

QatarEnergy, which operates Ras Laffan — the world’s largest LNG export plant — didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. [...] The effective closure of the key waterway near Iran and the Arabian Peninsula has choked off energy flows to global markets, disrupting about a fifth of the world’s supply of LNG. Another tanker, which appeared to not be carrying a shipment, passed through the strait over the weekend.

Qatar has delivered two LNG shipments to Kuwait over the past few weeks, according to ship-tracking data compiled by Kpler. These supplies were likely loading from Qatar’s storage tanks, and don’t require traversing Hormuz.

The company’s director of fertiliser markets, Terje Bakken, said companies and governments would give new thought to assessing the “vulnerabilities and risks of old supply systems”.

Bakken added that the risk of relying on fossil fuel sources “from geopolitically unstable regions to feed its population” is too high.

Atome is expected to issue a final investment decision (FID) on its 260,000 tonne per year fertiliser plant in the near term.

## Tighter market

Before the war, LNG export capacity was due to rise by 50 billion cubic metres per year. Under Fulwood’s most optimistic scenario, 2026 LNG supplies increase by only 12 bcm. [...] This scenario would allow Qatari and Emirati LNG supplies to return to the European Union in the third quarter. This would help the group meet its winter storage targets, which otherwise threaten to squeeze the world’s LNG market.

## Oil crunch

Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi both have alternative export routes avoiding Hormuz, but both have struggled.

Riyadh opted to export more via the East-West pipeline to the port of Yanbu. While nominal capacity on this link may be as high as 7 million barrels, it is constrained by loading capacity at the Red Sea terminal.

Abu Dhabi has built up capacity to bypass Hormuz by sending liquids to the port of Fujairah. But as Hormuz closed, Iran chose to launch attacks on Fujairah itself, squeezing exports. [...] ##### The first word in energy

# Hormuz reopens but ‘normal’ is gone for good

The ceasefire will run for two weeks, but the impact of the Middle Eastern war will reverberate for far longer

Ed Reed Editor

8 min read

April 9th 2026, 7:00 am

Powered by

 From our sister brand E-FWD, the UK's fastest-growing energy community. Every hub, every sector, every stage. Discover more

The fighting sides may have agreed that Hormuz is open with a two-week ceasefire. But, if the peace holds, what will the longer-term impact of this conflict be?

Some oilfields may not be able to return to flows recorded before the war, while damage to Qatar’s LNG facilities may need as much as five years to recover lost capacity.

results.content:
The Al Daayen and Rasheeda, which each loaded LNG from Qatar’s export plant in late-February, have now slowed and pulled back slightly after earlier heading eastward toward the opening of the strait near Oman, according to ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. It isn’t immediately clear from the data at this stage if the tankers will abandon the journey.
